quiz.0.question: What is the main reason Brunello and Chianti Classico have different vintage sensitivity?
quiz.0.options.1: Montalcino's higher elevation and drier climate make it more consistent; Chianti Classico's larger, more varied zone creates greater variation
quiz.0.options.2: Brunello has longer minimum ageing requirements
quiz.0.options.3: Chianti Classico uses many different grape varieties
quiz.0.explanation: Montalcino sits at higher elevations with a more consistently warm, dry microclimate — producing great vintages more reliably than the larger, more topographically diverse Chianti Classico zone.
quiz.1.question: What is the key stylistic difference between the great 2015 and 2016 vintages?
quiz.1.options.0: 2015 is a cool, austere year; 2016 is rich and opulent
quiz.1.options.1: 2015 is richer, more opulent and earlier-maturing; 2016 is more classically structured, higher in acidity and better for long ageing
quiz.1.options.2: Both vintages are identical in style
quiz.1.options.3: 2016 is a warm vintage; 2015 is a cold vintage
quiz.1.explanation: In Tuscany: 2015 was a warm year producing rich, plummy, earlier-drinkable wines. 2016 was the more 'perfect' vintage — combining ripeness with natural freshness and structure for maximum ageing.
quiz.2.question: In a warm Chianti Classico vintage, which sub-zone should you prioritise?
quiz.2.options.1: Panzano in Chianti or Radda in Chianti (higher elevation, cooler)
quiz.2.options.2: All sub-zones perform equally in warm years
quiz.2.explanation: In warm, ripe vintages, look to Chianti Classico's cooler higher-altitude sub-zones — Panzano, Radda in Chianti, Gaiole — where natural acidity is preserved better.
quiz.3.question: Which vintage purchasing strategy is most sensible for Tuscan wines?
quiz.3.options.1: Buy great vintages (2010, 2015, 2016) on release, then cellar — especially Brunello Riserva
quiz.3.options.2: Always buy the most recent vintage
quiz.3.options.3: Avoid Chianti Classico — it does not age
quiz.3.explanation: The same principle as Barolo: secure great vintages on release, cellar patiently. Brunello is released after 5 years and needs another 5–15 years. Chianti Classico Gran Selezione also ages superbly in great vintages.
